exam: Name the lakes and their claims: Seneca deepest and most wineries, Cayuga longest and first nested AVA, Keuka Y-shaped and Frank's lake.
Hold the dates: 1860 Pleasant Valley, 1953 Frank hired at Gold Seal, 1962 Vinifera Wine Cellars, 1976 Farm Winery Act, 1982 the AVA, 1988 Cayuga Lake, 2003 Seneca Lake.
Explain the lake effect twice: delayed bud break in spring, winter warmth on the slopes.
Know the Riesling styles and the sweetness scale of 2008.
Give the red: Cabernet Franc, with Lemberger beside it, and say why Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon struggle.
List the three families with an example of each: Concord, Cayuga White, Riesling.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: The flagship: lime, green apple, white peach and wet stone, high acidity and moderate alcohol, in dry, semi-dry, semi-sweet, late harvest and ice wine styles, often with the sweetness named on the label.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: The leading red vinifera, buds late and ripens early: raspberry, red currant, pepper and leaf, light to medium body, lightly oaked.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: Lychee, rose and ginger, dry to off-dry, a long-standing Finger Lakes speciality beside Riesling.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Lean, apple-scented wines and the base of traditional-method sparkling.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Light, bright reds from the warmest slopes and a sparkling component.

grapes.name: Blaufränkisch
grapes.styles: Grown as Lemberger: peppery, cold-hardy, medium-bodied red that ripens where Cabernet Sauvignon cannot.

grapes.name: Grüner Veltliner
grapes.styles: A recent arrival that suits the cool slopes: white pepper, green pear and crisp acidity.

grapes.name: Cayuga White
grapes.styles: The Cornell hybrid of 1972, named for the lake: crisp, fruity, off-dry white and sparkling.

grapes.name: Vidal Blanc
grapes.styles: A hardy hybrid for ice wine and off-dry whites.

grapes.name: Vignoles
grapes.styles: A botrytis-prone hybrid for sweet late-harvest wine.

grapes.name: Concord
grapes.styles: The native labrusca grape, still grown around the lakes for juice and sweet wine.

grapes.name: Catawba
grapes.styles: The pink native grape of the nineteenth-century sparkling houses at Hammondsport.

law.classification: The Finger Lakes AVA was approved in 1982 and covers the slopes around the lakes; Cayuga Lake, the region's first nested AVA, followed in 1988, and Seneca Lake in 2003. Like every AVA they state origin only. Federal rules govern the label: 75 per cent of the named grape, 85 per cent from the named AVA, 95 per cent from the stated vintage. Hybrids may be named like any variety at 75 per cent, and a labrusca grape such as Concord at 51 under a federal exception. A wine labelled ice wine must be made from grapes frozen naturally on the vine; the state's farm winery licence of 1976 requires New York fruit throughout. The Riesling sweetness scale on many labels is voluntary, not law.
labels: Sweetness words on a Riesling label, the house's own or the International Riesling Foundation's 2008 scale of dry, medium dry, medium sweet and sweet.
Sweet wine from fruit left to shrivel or take botrytis on the vine.
Grapes frozen on the vine and pressed frozen; the freezer is not allowed.
A Cornell hybrid of 1972 named for the lake.
Federal: grapes from the winery's own or controlled vineyards in the AVA, made and bottled there.
tiers: The state appellation: 75 per cent New York grapes.
The AVA of 1982: 85 per cent of the grapes from the slopes around the lakes.
The nested AVAs of 1988 and 2003, each a single lake's shores.
A licence, not a place: New York fruit only, direct sale allowed, the engine of the region since 1976.

made.viticulture: The first decision is the site, within reach of a lake and on a slope that drains cold air; the second is the winter. Growers mound soil over the graft union each autumn and pull it away in spring, so that a vine killed to the ground can regrow from the scion, and many train two or more trunks as insurance. Vertical shoot positioning is usual for vinifera; the native and hybrid grapes still hang on high wires in older systems. Rootstock is the Finger Lakes' founding idea: Frank's argument was that vinifera on hardy roots survives where own-rooted vines died. Rain falls through the growing season, so canopies are opened against mildew and botrytis, and the hybrids and natives earn their place by resisting both. Harvest is late and long, from September for the sparkling base into November for Riesling, and ice wine waits for a hard freeze, often into December or January, when the grapes are picked frozen, by custom at about minus eight degrees Celsius or lower. Deer and birds take their share; nets are common. The state agricultural experiment station at Geneva, founded in 1880 and Cornell's since 1923, breeds and trials the hybrids.
made.winemaking: Riesling is the craft. The fruit is pressed gently and fermented cool in stainless steel, dry or stopped by chilling to keep residual sugar, with the sweetness often declared on the label by the four-word scale the International Riesling Foundation introduced in 2008: dry, medium dry, medium sweet, sweet. Acidity is never short, so balance is the whole question. Late-harvest wines come from shrivelled or botrytised fruit, and ice wine from grapes frozen on the vine and pressed frozen, as federal rules require for the term. Cabernet Franc and Lemberger are fermented warm for colour and given modest, mostly used oak so the fruit and pepper lead. Sparkling wine is the region's oldest trade, traditional method since the Hammondsport houses of the 1860s, from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir and sometimes Riesling. The native grapes make juice, sweet and semi-sweet wine, and the hybrids crisp off-dry whites. Labels follow federal rules: 75 per cent of the named grape, 85 per cent from the AVA.

places.name: Seneca Lake
places.note: The deepest lake, about 188 metres (618 feet), and the one that almost never freezes, with the most wineries on its two shores; an AVA since 2003. The south-eastern shore is the banana belt, warmest ground in the region. Glenora opened the lake's first winery in 1977 and Hermann J. Wiemer planted at Dundee on the west shore in 1979; Watkins Glen sits at its southern tip.

places.name: Keuka Lake
places.note: The Y-shaped lake, with Hammondsport at its southern point: the cradle of the region, where Pleasant Valley made sparkling wine from 1860, Gold Seal hired Charles Fournier in 1934, and Konstantin Frank opened Vinifera Wine Cellars on the west shore in 1962. Cooler and shallower than Seneca; Riesling and sparkling wine.

places.name: Cayuga Lake
places.note: The longest lake, with Ithaca and Cornell at its southern end; the first nested AVA of the region, 1988. Vineyards line the west shore and the east, and the hybrid Cayuga White carries its name.

places.name: Canandaigua Lake
places.note: The westernmost wine lake, named in the 1945 founding of the Canandaigua Wine Company, which grew into Constellation Brands; Naples at its southern end is the old home of Widmer's and of labrusca wine.

places.name: Geneva
places.note: The town at the northern end of Seneca Lake and the home of the state agricultural experiment station, founded in 1880 and run by Cornell since 1923, which released Cayuga White and Traminette and still trials the region's grapes.

places.name: Hammondsport
places.note: The village at the southern tip of Keuka Lake where the region's wine trade began in the 1860s; Pleasant Valley's Great Western label was the first American sparkling wine to win a medal in Europe.

places.name: Skaneateles and the eastern lakes
places.note: The smaller lakes east of Cayuga, Owasco and Skaneateles among them, carry a few vineyards but little of the trade; the four western lakes hold nearly all of it.

producers.name: Dr. Konstantin Frank
producers.why: The house that proved vinifera could live in the east, founded as Vinifera Wine Cellars on Keuka Lake in 1962; Riesling, Gewürztraminer and sparkling wine still carry the name.

producers.name: Hermann J. Wiemer Vineyard
producers.why: Founded in 1979 at Dundee on Seneca Lake by a Mosel-born grower; its dry Rieslings are the region's benchmark and its nursery supplied vines across the east.

producers.name: Ravines Wine Cellars
producers.why: A dry-style house whose Rieslings and Cabernet Francs from Keuka and Seneca fruit set the modern standard for restraint.

producers.name: Red Newt Cellars
producers.why: A Seneca Lake east-shore house known for single-vineyard Rieslings of real depth.

producers.name: Fox Run Vineyards
producers.why: A west-shore Seneca estate with a long record in dry Riesling and Lemberger.

producers.name: Boundary Breaks
producers.why: A Seneca east-shore vineyard devoted almost entirely to Riesling, bottled by clone and by sweetness.

producers.name: Forge Cellars
producers.why: A Seneca Lake house founded with a Rhône partner, making dry Riesling and Pinot Noir in a European idiom.

producers.name: Heart and Hands Wine Company
producers.why: A Cayuga Lake specialist in Pinot Noir and Riesling from the cooler eastern shore.

producers.name: Glenora Wine Cellars
producers.why: Seneca Lake's first winery, opened in 1977 in the wake of the Farm Winery Act.

producers.name: Keuka Lake Vineyards
producers.why: A small Keuka house whose Rieslings and Vignoles show the cooler lake's edge.

sources.title: New York Wine and Grape Foundation, New York wine guide
Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau, Established American Viticultural Areas
International Riesling Foundation, the Riesling taste profile
The Oxford Companion to Wine, fifth edition

terroir.climate: Cool continental with a hard winter: the air can fall below minus 20 degrees Celsius, which kills vinifera buds and trunks, and only the lakes make the slopes habitable. The water stays cold into spring and delays bud break until the frosts have passed, then stays warm into autumn and winter and keeps the air above it a few degrees milder. Summers are warm and humid, rain falls in every month, and harvest runs from late September into November, with Riesling among the last picked. The season is short, so acidity stays high.
terroir.soils: Shale is the bedrock, laid down as sea mud in the Devonian age and lifted into the plateau the glaciers then cut. Over it lies glacial till, a mix of shale, gravel, silt and clay that the ice pushed and dropped, with limestone richer towards the lakes' northern ends. The slopes drain well where the till is gravelly and poorly where clay dominates, so site choice matters block by block. The shale gives the Riesling its wet-stone edge.
terroir.topography: The lakes run north to south, long and narrow, filling troughs the ice gouged into the plateau; the land rises in benches and slopes a hundred metres or more (several hundred feet) above the water. Vineyards sit on the slopes within two or three kilometres (a mile or two) of a lake, where the air drains downhill and the water's warmth reaches, and the best face east or west across the lake rather than away from it. Seneca is the deepest, Cayuga the longest, Keuka a Y with Hammondsport at its southern tip, Canandaigua the westernmost of the wine lakes.
terroir.water: Seneca Lake is about 188 metres (618 feet) deep and almost never freezes; Cayuga, at about 133 metres (435 feet), is the second deepest. Their mass is the region's thermostat, and the south-eastern shore of Seneca, warmest of all, is called the banana belt. Keuka and Canandaigua are shallower and cooler. The lakes drain north to Lake Ontario, which adds a second, broader moderation.

traps: Seneca is the deepest lake, Cayuga the longest; the two are close in length and the exam asks which is which.
Cayuga Lake was the first nested AVA (1988); Seneca Lake waited until 2003.
Dundee, near the west shore of Seneca Lake, is a New York village; Oregon's Dundee Hills are another place entirely.
Cayuga White is a hybrid, not a vinifera, and not a labrusca; Catawba and Concord are the natives.
Ice wine must freeze on the vine; the term is not for wines made from fruit frozen after picking.
The Riesling sweetness scale is voluntary; it is not a legal category like Germany's Prädikat ladder.
Frank's winery name is Vinifera Wine Cellars; the house is sold today under his own name.

wines.note: Lime, green apple and wet shale, bone dry, light and piercing; the region's finest wine. With oysters, trout, pork or Thai dishes.
Peach and apricot with a touch of sugar balanced by acidity; the style most guests know and the one for spicy food.
Honeyed, apricot-scented dessert wine from shrivelled or botrytised fruit; with fruit tarts or blue cheese.
Grapes frozen on the vine and pressed frozen: intense, sweet, electric with acidity, in half bottles. A small pour after dinner.
Raspberry, red currant, pepper and a leafy edge, light to medium body, modest oak; serve a little cool with duck, pork or mushrooms.
Lychee, rose and ginger, off-dry; with spiced dishes and soft cheese.
Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and sometimes Riesling or Cayuga White, aged on lees; the region's oldest trade, from the Hammondsport houses of the 1860s.
Peppery, bright and medium-bodied Blaufränkisch under its local name; with sausages and roast pork.

exam: Lead with the water: Sound, Peconic Bay, Atlantic; the longest season in the state; Merlot ripens.
Hold the dates: 1973 the first vinifera at Cutchogue, 1985 The Hamptons AVA, 1986 North Fork AVA, 2001 Long Island AVA.
Name the grapes in order: Merlot, then Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc.
Tell the two forks apart: North warmer, drier, most vines, Merlot; South cooler, foggier, rosé and whites.
Know the hazards: humidity, fungus, autumn hurricanes, and the sandy outwash soil that drains them away.
Carry the federal percentages and Meritage.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The most planted grape and the island's signature: plum, red cherry, soft tannin and moderate alcohol, closer to a Bordeaux Merlot than to a Californian one.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Fragrant, red-fruited and leafy, blended with Merlot or bottled alone; the island's most distinctive red after Merlot.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The leading white, from steely unoaked bottlings to barrel-fermented wines and traditional-method sparkling.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Ripens only in the warmer years and sites; a blending partner in the Bordeaux-style reds rather than a lead.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Grassy, citrus-driven whites that suit the island's seafood.

grapes.name: Petit Verdot
grapes.styles: A seasoning grape in the Bordeaux-style blends, dark and firm.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: A small planting, blended or bottled alone by a few houses.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: A few dry and off-dry bottlings from the cooler sites.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: A rarity on the North Fork, dry and apple-scented, that one house has made a speciality.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Mostly for sparkling base on the cooler South Fork.

grapes.name: Albariño
grapes.styles: A recent planting that suits the maritime air: saline, citrus whites for the shellfish table.

law.classification: Three AVAs cover the island, each stating origin only. The Hamptons, Long Island came first in 1985 for the South Fork; the North Fork of Long Island followed in 1986; and the island-wide Long Island AVA of 2001 takes in both forks and the whole of Nassau and Suffolk counties, so that a wine blended across the forks has a name. Federal rules govern the label: 75 per cent of the named grape, 85 per cent from the named AVA, 95 per cent from the stated vintage. New York adds no stricter rule; the farm winery licence of 1976 requires New York fruit throughout and allows direct sale. Meritage is a trademarked term used under licence for a blend of two or more Bordeaux grapes with none above 90 per cent, coined for blends that could not carry a varietal name.
labels: The warmer fork; Merlot and the Bordeaux blends.
The South Fork; rosé, whites and sparkling.
A trademarked term for a Bordeaux-style blend; a licence, not a law.
Federal: grapes from the winery's own or controlled vineyards in the AVA, made and bottled there.
tiers: The state appellation: 75 per cent New York grapes.
The island-wide AVA of 2001, both forks and the whole of Nassau and Suffolk counties.
The AVA of 1986 on the warmer northern fork, from Riverhead to Orient Point; most of the vines.
The AVA of 1985 on the cooler South Fork, from Bridgehampton to Sagaponack and beyond.
A licence, not a place: New York fruit only, direct sale allowed.

made.viticulture: The island's growers farm against humidity. Vines are trained on vertical shoot positioning with open canopies, leaves are pulled from the fruit zone, and rows run to catch the sea breeze so the clusters dry after rain; sprays against mildew and botrytis are routine and the regional sustainability programme, Long Island Sustainable Winegrowing, has certified estates since 2012. The sandy outwash soils drain fast and hold little water, so vigour is naturally moderate and some blocks are drip irrigated in a dry July. Yields are kept modest for the reds. Harvest begins with sparkling base and Sauvignon Blanc in September and runs through Merlot and Cabernet Franc in October into early November, among the latest in the state, and the long season is both the region's gift and its gamble: a hurricane or a wet autumn can undo it. Birds and deer are netted and fenced against. The North Fork, warmer and drier, carries most of the vines; the South Fork's cooler, foggier sites lean to rosé, sparkling and whites. Cabernet Sauvignon is planted on the warmest blocks and still ripens only in good years.
made.winemaking: The model is Bordeaux. Merlot and its partners are destemmed, fermented in stainless or small open tanks with moderate extraction, pressed to French oak with a modest share new, and aged twelve to eighteen months; the blends are assembled in the Bordeaux manner and several estates make a Merlot-led flagship under a proprietary name. The Long Island Merlot Alliance, formed in 2005, promoted the grape as the island's signature. Cabernet Franc is handled more gently to keep its perfume. Chardonnay runs from stainless steel to barrel fermentation with lees stirring; Sauvignon Blanc is cool-fermented in steel. Rosé, direct pressed and pale, became the South Fork's volume wine. Traditional-method sparkling has grown into a speciality, aged on lees for years. The federal rules apply: 75 per cent of the named grape, 85 per cent from the named AVA, 95 per cent from the stated vintage, and Meritage, under licence, for a blend of two or more Bordeaux grapes with none above 90 per cent.

places.name: North Fork of Long Island
places.note: The narrow northern fork from Riverhead to Orient Point, an AVA since 1986 and the home of most of the island's vines: warmer and drier than the South Fork, with the Sound on one side and the Peconic Bay on the other. Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc on sandy loam that was potato ground until 1973.

places.name: Cutchogue
places.note: The hamlet where the first vinifera vineyard was planted on a potato farm in 1973, said to be the sunniest spot in the state; Bedell and the original 1973 site, now Castello di Borghese, are here.

places.name: Mattituck and Jamesport
places.note: The western hamlets of the North Fork, with Macari, Paumanok and Jamesport Vineyards among the estates along the main road and the Sound shore.

places.name: Peconic and Southold
places.note: The eastern hamlets towards Greenport and Orient Point, cooler and more exposed, with Lenz, Pindar and Sparkling Pointe among the estates.

places.name: The Hamptons, Long Island
places.note: The South Fork, an AVA since 1985, where the Atlantic keeps the season cooler and foggier: Bridgehampton, Sagaponack and Water Mill hold the vineyards, Wölffer Estate and Channing Daughters the famous names, and rosé, whites and sparkling the strengths. The Bridgehampton silt loam is its soil.

places.name: Peconic Bay
places.note: The sheltered water between the forks, warm in autumn and the source of the North Fork's long season; its oysters, clams and scallops are the island's natural pairing.

places.name: Riverhead
places.note: The town at the base of the forks where the island divides, the western edge of the North Fork AVA and the gateway from the city.

producers.name: Bedell Cellars
producers.why: A Cutchogue estate from 1980 whose Merlot and Bordeaux-style blends defined the North Fork's serious end.

producers.name: Lenz Winery
producers.why: Planted in 1978 at Peconic; long-aged Merlot and Chardonnay that first put North Fork wines beside Bordeaux at blind tastings.

producers.name: Paumanok Vineyards
producers.why: A family estate at Aquebogue since 1983, known for Chenin Blanc, Riesling and Bordeaux-style reds.

producers.name: Macari Vineyards
producers.why: A Mattituck estate planted in 1995 on the Sound, farmed with biodynamic methods; Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc.

producers.name: Wölffer Estate
producers.why: The South Fork's landmark at Sagaponack, planted from 1988; its pale rosé became the Hamptons' summer wine and its Merlot and Chardonnay are serious.

producers.name: Channing Daughters
producers.why: A Bridgehampton house known for unusual whites, Italian varieties and skin-contact wines on the South Fork.

producers.name: Sparkling Pointe
producers.why: A Southold house devoted to traditional-method sparkling wine from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier.

producers.name: Pindar Vineyards
producers.why: One of the island's largest and oldest estates, at Peconic since 1979, with a wide range from Merlot to sweet wines.

producers.name: Castello di Borghese
producers.why: The original vineyard at Cutchogue, planted in 1973, the island's first vinifera site under a later name.

producers.name: Shinn Estate Vineyards
producers.why: A Mattituck estate known for sustainable farming and Merlot-led blends.

Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau, Established American Viticultural Areas
Code of Federal Regulations, Title 27, Part 4, labelling of wine
The Oxford Companion to Wine, fifth edition

terroir.climate: Maritime and mild: water on three sides holds off spring frost, slows the summer heat and extends the autumn, so the frost-free season on the North Fork runs past two hundred days and Merlot and even Cabernet Sauvignon can finish in October. The price is humidity, which breeds mildew and botrytis, and the Atlantic hurricane season, which can strip a vineyard in September. The South Fork is cooler, fog-prone and later than the North, because the ocean lies directly beside it.
terroir.soils: Sandy loam over glacial outwash, deposited as the last ice sheet melted: the Haven and Riverhead soils of the North Fork and the Bridgehampton silt loam of the South Fork are the names the growers use. They drain fast, hold little water and less nutrient, which restrains vigour in a humid place, and some blocks are irrigated in a dry summer. Gravel and pebbles run through them; there is no bedrock within reach of a root.
terroir.topography: Flat and low. The island's spine is the pair of terminal moraines the ice left behind, one along each fork, and the vineyards lie on the gentle outwash plain between the moraine and the water, mostly under 30 metres (a hundred feet) above the sea. The North Fork is a narrow strip of farmland some 50 kilometres (thirty miles) long from Riverhead to Orient Point; the South Fork, the Hamptons, is wider and more built up, with vineyards around Bridgehampton, Sagaponack and Water Mill.
terroir.water: Long Island Sound to the north, the Peconic Bay between the forks, the Atlantic Ocean to the south. The Sound and the bay warm slowly in spring and cool slowly in autumn, which is the whole secret of the North Fork; the open Atlantic makes the South Fork cooler and foggier. Sea breezes dry the canopy after rain, the region's one defence against fungus.

traps: The Hamptons AVA (1985) is older than the North Fork AVA (1986); the island-wide AVA came only in 2001.
Merlot, not Cabernet Sauvignon, leads Long Island; Cabernet Sauvignon ripens only on the warmest blocks in good years.
Long Island is maritime and the Finger Lakes are continental; the winter kill that rules the lakes is not the island's problem.
The soils are sand and gravel over outwash with no bedrock; there is no shale, no limestone and no Jory here.
Cutchogue is on the North Fork; Sagaponack and Bridgehampton are on the South Fork.
The island-wide Long Island AVA covers the whole of Nassau and Suffolk counties, not only the forks.

wines.note: Plum, red cherry, a little earth and tobacco, soft tannin, medium body; the island's calling card. Serve with duck, roast lamb or a mushroom dish.
Merlot with Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Petit Verdot and Malbec, often under a proprietary name or Meritage; the prestige bottling of most estates. With steak or a rich braise.
Raspberry, red currant, pepper and a leafy note, lighter than the blends; serve a touch cool with pork or grilled vegetables.
From crisp and unoaked to barrel-fermented and creamy; with lobster, scallops or roast chicken.
Grassy, grapefruit and sea air, dry and brisk; with oysters and clams from the same bays.
Pale, dry, strawberry-scented rosé from Merlot and the other Bordeaux grapes, the South Fork's summer wine; chilled, with anything on a terrace.
Chardonnay and Pinot Noir aged on lees, a growing speciality of a few North Fork houses; as an aperitif or with fried seafood.

exam: Open with the three families: labrusca (Concord, Catawba, Niagara), French-American hybrids (Vidal, Seyval, Cayuga White), vinifera (Riesling, Cabernet Franc, Merlot).
Tell Frank's story in two lines: hired at Gold Seal in 1953, vinifera on hardy rootstock, Vinifera Wine Cellars on Keuka Lake in 1962.
Hold the dates: Brotherhood 1839, Farm Winery Act 1976, Finger Lakes AVA 1982, the first Cutchogue vineyard 1973, Long Island AVA 2001.
Explain the lake effect: deep water delays spring bud break, extends autumn and keeps the slopes above a killing freeze.
Pair the wines: Finger Lakes Riesling, Long Island Merlot, Cabernet Franc in both, Concord on Lake Erie.
Know the eleven AVAs and which nest inside which.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: The state's flagship vinifera, from the Finger Lakes: dry, semi-dry, late harvest and ice wine, lime and peach with keen acidity.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: The red vinifera that ripens where Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon struggle: fragrant, leafy, bright, in the Finger Lakes and on Long Island.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Long Island's leading grape, soft and plummy in the long maritime autumn of the North Fork.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Grown everywhere vinifera is, from lean Finger Lakes bottlings to fuller Long Island wines and traditional-method sparkling.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: A Finger Lakes speciality beside Riesling, lychee and rose, off-dry to dry.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Light reds and sparkling base from the cooler Finger Lakes sites.

grapes.name: Blaufränkisch
grapes.styles: Sold as Lemberger; a peppery, cold-hardy red the Finger Lakes have grown for decades.

grapes.name: Concord
grapes.styles: The labrusca grape of the Lake Erie juice belt, the most planted vine in the state by far; juice, jelly and sweet wine, foxy in aroma.

grapes.name: Cayuga White
grapes.styles: A Cornell hybrid released in 1972 for crisp, fruity, off-dry white and sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Vidal Blanc
grapes.styles: A hardy French-American hybrid grown for ice wine and off-dry whites.

labels: The AVA of 1982 around eleven glacial lakes; Riesling country.
The two nested Finger Lakes AVAs, 2003 and 1988.
The AVA of 1986 on the warmer, drier northern fork; Merlot country.
The AVA of 1985 on the cooler South Fork, cooled by the Atlantic.
The sweetness words a Finger Lakes Riesling label often carries; the International Riesling Foundation's scale of 2008 uses dry, medium dry, medium sweet and sweet.
Wine from grapes frozen on the vine and pressed frozen; grapes frozen after picking may not use the term.
Hybrids released by Cornell's Geneva station, Cayuga White in 1972 and Traminette in 1996; a hybrid may be named on the label like any grape.
Native labrusca grapes, foxy in aroma, mostly for juice and sweet wine.
The name under which Blaufränkisch is often sold in the Finger Lakes.
ladder: 75 per cent of the grapes from New York under federal law; the state adds no stricter rule.

Origin only: Finger Lakes (1982), Hudson River Region (1982), Lake Erie (1983), Long Island (2001), Niagara Escarpment (2005), Champlain Valley of New York (2016), Upper Hudson; 85 per cent of the grapes from inside the named area.
Cayuga Lake (1988) and Seneca Lake (2003) inside the Finger Lakes; North Fork of Long Island (1986) and The Hamptons, Long Island (1985) inside Long Island.
A licence under the 1976 Act, not an appellation: wine made from New York fruit only, sold directly to the public.
75 per cent of the named grape for vinifera and hybrids; a labrusca variety such as Concord may be named at 51 per cent under a federal exception.
new-york.overview:
Huguenot settlers planted vines at New Paltz in the Hudson Valley in 1677, and Brotherhood Winery at Washingtonville, founded in 1839, is the oldest continuously operating winery in the United States. The Finger Lakes followed in the 1860s with the Pleasant Valley Wine Company at Hammondsport, the first bonded winery in the country, and the Urbana company that became Gold Seal, both making sparkling wine from Catawba and other native grapes. Prohibition left the state growing Concord for juice and jelly, and the dry wine that returned after 1933 was mostly hybrid. The turn came at Gold Seal, where Charles Fournier, who had come from Veuve Clicquot in 1934, hired the Ukrainian-born émigré Konstantin Frank in 1953. Frank argued that vinifera failed in the east not from cold but from the wrong roots, grafted Riesling and Chardonnay onto hardy rootstock, and in 1962 opened Vinifera Wine Cellars on Keuka Lake. Long Island's first vinifera went into a former potato farm at Cutchogue in 1973. The Farm Winery Act of 1976 let small growers make and sell their own wine directly, and the number of wineries climbed from a handful to several hundred.

The geography is water against winter. The climate is continental, with winters that drop well below the point at which vinifera buds and trunks die, so every region leans on a body of water deep or wide enough to blunt the cold. The Finger Lakes are glacial troughs that hold summer heat into winter and delay bud break in spring; Lake Erie and Lake Ontario shelter the western shore and the Niagara Escarpment; the Hudson is tidal to Troy and tempers its valley; Long Island has the Sound, the Peconic Bay and the Atlantic on three sides and the longest season in the state. Lake Erie holds the most acreage, nearly all of it Concord; the Finger Lakes hold most of the wineries and the reputation.

The law is federal: 75 per cent of the named grape, 85 per cent from a named AVA, 95 per cent from a stated vintage on an AVA wine. The state's eleven AVAs are the Finger Lakes with Cayuga Lake and Seneca Lake inside it, Lake Erie shared with Pennsylvania and Ohio, the Hudson River Region and Upper Hudson, Long Island with the North Fork and The Hamptons inside it, the Niagara Escarpment and the Champlain Valley of New York. A farm winery licence requires wine made from New York fruit alone, which is a licence condition, not an appellation. Ice wine labelled as such must come from grapes frozen on the vine.

The exam leans on Finger Lakes Riesling, the lake effect, Frank's 1962 proof, the three families of vine, Cabernet Franc as the eastern red, Long Island Merlot and its maritime season, and the Farm Winery Act.

traps: Lake Erie, not the Finger Lakes, holds most of New York's vineyard acreage; nearly all of it is Concord for juice.
Cabernet Franc, not Cabernet Sauvignon, is the eastern red that ripens reliably; Merlot ripens on Long Island but struggles in the Finger Lakes.
Dundee, New York, is a Finger Lakes village near the west shore of Seneca Lake; Dundee, Oregon, is in the Willamette Valley.
The Hamptons AVA of 1985 came before the North Fork AVA of 1986, and the island-wide Long Island AVA only in 2001.
Ice wine is frozen on the vine; a sweet wine from grapes frozen in a freezer may not carry the term.
New York adds nothing to federal label percentages; the 90 per cent rule is Oregon's.
